title: How School Trains You to Burn Out
author: Katy Purviance
summary: Purviance argues that school does not cause adult burnout directly but trains the behaviors that make it almost unavoidable once sustained pressure arrives. She works through six symptoms of severe burnout and traces each to a specific feature of schooling: the bell that overrides a child's own sense of when something is finished, permission rules for basic bodily needs, grades that replace an internal sense of enough with an external verdict, constant observation, deference to the expert at the front of the room, and approval for being quiet and undemanding. She supports the argument with Stephen Porges on neuroception, Alfie Kohn on grades, John Taylor Gatto on the hidden curriculum, Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory, and Peter Gray on school as a source of youth distress. The result, she claims, is a nervous system that cannot tell dedication from self-destruction and only registers exhaustion once it becomes catastrophic. She closes with three small practices, a body check, an origin sentence and a count of the invisible evaluator, as first steps toward relearning one's own signals.
points: Purviance argues years of bell schedules teach children to stop checking their own internal stopping point.
She links hand raising for bathroom and water breaks to adults who feel guilty and restless even on a sick day.
Grades, she contends, train people to wait for collapse before they consider their exhaustion real.
Drawing on self-determination theory, she argues reliance on external validation erodes trust in one's own read of fatigue.
Her practical exercises ask readers to notice bodily yes and no signals and to count moments of performing for an absent evaluator.
quotes: School does not cause burnout directly. It trains the exact behaviors that make burnout almost impossible to avoid once sustained pressure sets in.
That training produces a nervous system that cannot tell the difference between dedication and self-destruction.

Across thirteen years, that lesson repeats thousands of times, until a person stops checking in with their own internal stopping point at all, because the schedule was always going to override it anyway.
None of these requests were actually requests. They were procedures, and the procedure taught a child that even the most basic bodily needs required someone else’s approval first.

Grades were supposed to measure how well you learned the material, and sometimes they did. What they did more reliably, and far more permanently, was replace a child’s own internal sense of enough with an external verdict.
Rest starts to feel like exposure, like the moment someone will finally notice you were not working hard enough.
A system built on rewarding the override of your own limits, and punishing the admission of them, trained you to distrust the one signal that could have told you when to stop.
